title: Clean and hexagonal architecture
subtitle: Learn how to keep business rules apart from the web framework and the database, why tests get faster, and when the extra layers are not worth it.

c.v: This story is made up, but each part is common. Ravi works on the orders service of an online pharmacy. The
handler is 250 lines long. It reads the JSON body, checks the prescription rules, applies discounts and writes SQL to save the order.
The rules for prescription drugs changed. Ravi only needed to change one check. But the check sat between an Express
. To test it, he had to start a server and a real Postgres in Docker.
The test suite took 14 minutes. People stopped running it before they pushed. Two weeks later, a discount bug reached production. Nobody had run the test that would have caught it.

Then the company wanted orders from a nightly CSV import too. The rules lived inside the HTTP handler, so the import team copied them. Now the same rules existed in two places, and they slowly drifted apart.
The business rules were tangled with HTTP and SQL. That made them slow to test and hard to reuse.

The six sides mean nothing. Cockburn writes that "the number six" is not important. The shape just leaves room to draw more ports.
Put the business rules in a core that imports no framework and no database driver. The core owns its interfaces. Everything outside depends on the core, never the other way round.

Cockburn splits the outside world in two. A primary actor "drives the application", such as a user or a test. A secondary actor is one "that the application drives", such as a database.
He says you can also call them driving adapters and driven adapters.
Ports come in the same two kinds.
The core: a use case and a port
A use case is one thing a user can do, such as "place an order".
is the driving port: the API the core offers to the outside. Some teams also write it as an interface. The core also defines the driven port it needs, in its own words.
The adapter turns HTTP into a call, and a core error into a status code. The CSV import from the story becomes a second driving adapter. It calls the same
method. The rules now live in one place.

So the three names share one idea. Business rules sit in the middle. Frameworks and databases are details at the edge. Dependencies point inward.

One feature now needs a use case, a port, two adapters and the wiring. For simple features, that is a lot of reading.
Martin wants data to cross in the inner circle's form.
So you often copy fields from a request object to a core type, and from a core type to a database row. Each copy is code to write and test.

CRUD means create, read, update and delete: screens that only save and load rows, with few rules. Palermo says his design "is not appropriate for small websites". He aims it at long-lived business apps and at apps with complex behaviour.
If a screen just saves a form to a table, the core has nothing to protect.

Jimmy Bogard says layered, onion and clean designs are "really only appropriate in a minority of the typical requests in a system".
He says he tends to see them as "mock-heavy, with rigid rules around dependency management".
He adds that one feature often means "touching many different 'layers'".
You do not need the full design everywhere. Start with a clean core only for the part with real rules, such as pricing or order limits. Leave simple CRUD screens simple. Inside a
, each module can make this choice for itself.
Bogard's team once started a long project with an onion architecture. Within a couple of months, problems showed, and they moved away from it, towards
groups code by request, not by layer. His rule: "Minimize coupling between slices, and maximize coupling in a slice."
Each slice "can decide for itself how to best fulfill the request".
A simple slice can use SQL directly. A complex one can have a rich core.
It has a cost too. Bogard says it assumes "your team understands code smells and refactoring".
Without that, logic can grow messy inside each slice.

sections.title: At work: how a senior uses this

c.v: Ask: "Can I test this rule without a server or a database?" If not, the rule is tangled with a detail.

Check the imports. Code in the core should not import the web framework, the ORM or the SQL driver. Tools such as dependency-cruiser or eslint-plugin-boundaries (TypeScript) and ArchUnit (Java) can check this in
Add a port only at a real edge, and name its second adapter, often the test one.
Keep one integration test per driven adapter against the real tool.
Before you add layers to a CRUD screen, count its business rules. If there are none, keep it simple.
When an entry point is added (a queue consumer, a CLI, a cron job), make it a new driving adapter. Do not copy the rules.
"List every file under src/core that imports express, pg, an ORM or an HTTP client. For each import, say what the core uses it for."
"Find business rules that appear in more than one HTTP handler or job. Show the duplicated lines side by side."
"Extract the order limit rule from this handler into a PlaceOrder use case with an OrderRepository port. Add an in-memory adapter and one unit test. Do not change the HTTP behaviour."
The core has no imports from framework or database packages.
The port uses business words, not table or column names.
The agent did not add an interface for every class inside the core.
The in-memory adapter behaves like the real one for the cases you test. A real-database integration test still exists.
The HTTP status codes and JSON shape did not change.

q.v: In Clean Architecture, which direction may source code dependencies point?

options.v: Outward, from the business rules to the database and framework.
Both ways, as long as each layer has interfaces.

why.v: Martin's dependency rule says source code dependencies "can only point inwards".

q.v: Your PlaceOrder use case needs to save orders. Where does the OrderRepository interface belong?

options.v: In the core, next to PlaceOrder, written in the core's words.
In the Postgres package, next to the SQL code.
In the HTTP controller, which creates everything.

why.v: The core owns the port. Palermo also puts repository interfaces in the core and their implementations at the edge.

q.v: An HTTP handler and a unit test both call PlaceOrder. In Cockburn's words, what are they?

options.v: Driving (primary) adapters, because they start the work.

why.v: Cockburn calls an actor that drives the application primary, and also uses the name driving adapters.

q.v: An admin tool only reads and writes rows in 6 tables, with almost no rules. What is a reasonable design?

options.v: Full hexagonal layers with mappers for each table.
A simple design that talks to the database directly, because there is little core to protect.

why.v: Palermo says his design is "not appropriate for small websites". With few rules, the layers cost more than they save.

q.v: Your unit tests use an in-memory adapter. What else do you still need?

options.v: Nothing. The in-memory adapter proves the SQL works.
A few integration tests that run the Postgres adapter against a real PostgreSQL.

why.v: The fake does not run your SQL at all. Even an in-memory SQL database is "risky business", Vocke warns, because it differs from production.
